passage: Swati, you asked why I always give the Kamble girls a lift in the rain. Let me tell you. When your Madhuri Nani was ten, in Nashik, our driver took me to school in a white car, even in the worst monsoon. One morning, splashing along the river road, I saw my classmate Sunanda walking, her schoolbag on her head, her skirt soaked to the knees. She walked five kilometres every day. I had never once thought about it. That night I asked my father, "Why does she walk and I don't?" He said, "Some people are luckier, that's all." I felt guilty, then cross, as if it were my fault. The next week I asked if Sunanda could ride with me. My father went quiet. Then he said yes.

qa.q: How far did Sunanda walk to school every day?
qa.a: Five kilometres.

qa.q: How did young Madhuri feel after her father's answer?
qa.a: She felt guilty and then cross, as if the difference were her own fault, and kept wondering why it was so.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned Madhuri's question into action?
qa.a: Asking her father if Sunanda could ride with her in the car, which shared a little of her head start.

qa.q: What might the car ride have meant to Sunanda?
qa.a: It probably meant a dry, less tiring start to the day, though she may also have felt shy accepting a lift from a richer classmate.

grounding: A child who rides to school by car notices a classmate walking far in the rain, asks why and feels guilty and defensive.

subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Gopika Ma'am,
It's the Christmas break and the hostel is almost empty, so I'm finally writing.
First semester was hard in ways I didn't expect. Half my class had coaching since Class 8. When a professor mentioned an internship, three of them said, "Oh, my uncle's firm does that," and had places by Friday. One classmate failed a subject and said, "Papa will just pay for the re-exam and a summer course." I sat there doing sums in my head: bus fare, hostel fees, Abbu's shop.
Honestly, I felt bitter. Same race, but they started halfway down the track.
Then results came. I got a B-plus in the hardest paper, on library books and your old notes. I cried in the washroom, happy this time.
I'm proud of the distance I've covered, Ma'am. Please tell the Class 10 students.
Farida

qa.q: What grade did Farida get in the hardest paper?
qa.a: A B-plus.

qa.q: How does Farida feel about the classmates with coaching and uncles' firms?
qa.a: Farida feels bitter and resentful, as if they started the same race halfway down the track.

qa.q: What could Farida do to reach the openings others found through family?
qa.a: Farida could ask professors and the placement office directly about internships, and stay in touch with mentors like Gopika Ma'am.

qa.q: How might Gopika Ma'am feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Gopika Ma'am would likely feel proud and moved, seeing old notes help Farida cover such a distance.

grounding: A student from a modest background sees classmates' coaching, connections and safety nets and feels both resentment and pride in how far they have come.

passage: Salma was the only one from her kasba in Beed district who had gone to an English-medium school and then to college in Pune, thanks to her father's clinic and her uncle's contacts. Back home now, running a women's savings-group office for an NGO, she knew it. When a paid training post in accounts opened, her cousin's friend phoned to ask for it. Salma asked the women's group instead why so few of them applied for such posts. "The forms are always in English," said Manjula, who had kept the group ledger for three years in careful Marathi. So Salma put the notice on the panchayat wall and the group chat in Marathi, and at the interview she translated the English forms herself. Manjula got the post. "You didn't have to do all that," Manjula said. "I did," Salma said. "Someone did it for me."

qa.q: How long had Manjula kept the group ledger?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What does Salma's reply "Someone did it for me" suggest about how she sees her advantage?
qa.a: She feels grateful rather than guilty, seeing her head start clearly and wanting to pass it on.

qa.q: Which of Salma's steps made the hiring fair?
qa.a: Asking the women what held them back, posting the notice in Marathi where everyone could see it, and translating the English forms so Manjula was judged on skill.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Salma's help?
qa.a: Manjula is surprised and grateful, since the extra effort let her ledger skills count instead of her English.

grounding: A young adult who knows her head start came from family and language listens to those with less and opens a job fairly, without guilt or denial.

passage: On the day after Sports Day in December, Kiran counted medals before the first bell. He had one silver, for the sack race. Suraj had two golds. Priyank had none at all. Kiran felt taller than Priyank and smaller than Suraj, both in the same minute. In art period he peeked at everyone's drawing of a winter tree before colouring his own. Suraj's tree had snow, somehow, in Mumbai. Kiran's tree suddenly looked flat. He rubbed it out. "Why did you do that?" asked Miss Joseph. "Suraj's is better." "I asked for your tree, not Suraj's," she said. At home, Kiran pinned the silver medal on his school bag, then took it off, then pinned it on again.

qa.q: Which race did Kiran win silver in?
qa.a: The sack race.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when he counted the medals?
qa.a: He felt proud next to Priyank and small next to Suraj, both in the same minute.

qa.q: What could help Kiran enjoy his own work more?
qa.a: He could look at his own tree before anyone else's and compare it with his earlier drawings, as Miss Joseph hinted 🙂.

qa.q: Why might Miss Joseph have said "I asked for your tree"?
qa.a: She wants Kiran to value his own effort instead of ranking himself against Suraj.

grounding: A child checks classmates' medals and drawings and feels proud or small by turns, letting the ranking colour his own work.

passage: Saurabh, put the phone down for one minute and let your Jeevan chacha tell you something. The summer I was sixteen, Nagpur was forty-six degrees and I was stuck at home. Every night I lay under the fan scrolling. Rohit in Manali, in snow. Anjali at a science camp. Some boy from my class holding a guitar trophy. My life was power cuts and my mother's lauki. I felt so dull I stopped replying to anyone. Then in July Rohit came back. On the terrace he admitted the Manali trip was three days of car sickness and a fight with his dad; he had posted the one good photo. That night I understood: I had been comparing my every ordinary day with everyone's single best minute. So I started a small notebook of my own good minutes. Guess who still has it.

qa.q: How hot was Nagpur that summer?
qa.a: Forty-six degrees.

qa.q: How did young Jeevan feel while scrolling every night?
qa.a: He felt dull and left behind, so low that he stopped replying to anyone.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Jeevan?
qa.a: Starting a small notebook of his own good minutes, after realising he was comparing ordinary days with others' single best moments.

qa.q: What might Rohit have felt posting the one good photo from Manali?
qa.a: Rohit may have wanted to hide a disappointing trip and look happy, with private embarrassment behind the snowy picture.

grounding: A teenager scrolling friends' holiday highlights feels dull and behind until he sees he is comparing ordinary days with others' best moments.

passage:
Monday, the week of Christmas. Rohini, their batchmate, posts: "Summer internship at the design studio! 🎉" In the canteen Samir says, "How did she get that? I want to know." Jaya says nothing and stirs her tea.
Thursday. Samir messages Rohini, asks what her portfolio had, and spends the evening redoing his own. Jaya opens Rohini's profile eleven times, then her own, and types in her notes: "Behind. Always behind. Why bother."
New Year's Eve. Samir sends out three applications, a little scared but buzzing. Jaya hasn't opened her portfolio file. When Samir asks, she snaps, "Easy for you, you're good at this." He sits down beside her. "Rohini said she got rejected six times first. Want to look at yours together?" Jaya hesitates, then nods.

qa.q: How many times did Jaya open Rohini's profile?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she typed "Behind. Always behind"?
qa.a: She felt envious and hopeless, sinking into self-criticism as if Rohini's goal were out of reach for her.

qa.q: What did Samir do that turned the comparison into motivation?
qa.a: He asked Rohini what her portfolio had and redid his own, treating her success as a reachable path, then shared that she had been rejected six times first.

qa.q: How might Rohini's six rejections change how Jaya sees the internship?
qa.a: They could make the goal feel reachable, showing Rohini struggled too, so Jaya might compare with hope instead of despair.

grounding: Two students see a friend's internship: one is spurred to work harder, the other sinks into envy until the goal starts to look reachable.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage: It was Onam week in Pala, and the bank branch had a flower carpet in the lobby when Joseph got the call: promoted to assistant manager. Everyone clapped. Hemant clapped too, his smile a little stiff. They had joined the same week three years ago and shared a rented room above the tailor's shop. Hemant was glad. He was also, he found, stung, a small sharp feeling he didn't like. He kept himself busy with the sadya leaves at lunch. That evening on the roof, Joseph asked, "You okay? You went quiet." Hemant almost said "Fine." Instead: "Honestly? I'm really happy for you, and I'm a bit jealous, and I hate that I'm jealous." Joseph laughed, relieved. "I'd be jealous too." Then Hemant hugged him properly, the congratulations finally real.

qa.q: What was Joseph promoted to?
qa.a: Assistant manager.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel when Joseph's promotion was announced?
qa.a: He felt glad for Joseph and also stung and jealous, which made his smile stiff.

qa.q: Why did telling Joseph the truth help?
qa.a: Admitting both happiness and jealousy cleared the hidden awkwardness, so Hemant's hug and congratulations could be genuine 🤍.

qa.q: How did Joseph react when Hemant admitted the jealousy?
qa.a: Joseph felt relieved and laughed, saying he would be jealous too, glad the quiet was explained.

grounding: A young adult feels happy and stung at a close friend's promotion, admits the mixed feelings and can then congratulate him genuinely.

passage:
Hi Chinmay,
You asked how I'm handling the batch reunion group, where everyone seems to be a founder or living in Berlin. Here's what I've done.
First, I muted the three accounts that left me low every single time. I didn't unfollow; I just stopped looking.
Second, I dug out my notes from a year ago. Then: scared of client calls, couldn't read a balance sheet, rent late twice. Now: I lead two client accounts and paid rent on time all year. That's not Berlin, but it's real.
Third, I picked three people I actually learn from, you included, and I ask them real questions instead of just watching their posts. Nidhi is teaching me to negotiate.
I still compare. I'm just choosing what with.
Write back with your own a-year-ago list.
Kamal

qa.q: How many accounts did Kamal mute?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel about the reunion group before muting accounts?
qa.a: Kamal felt low and behind, since everyone seemed to be a founder or living in Berlin.

qa.q: Which of Kamal's steps keeps the useful side of comparison?
qa.a: Choosing a few people to learn from and asking them real questions, like Nidhi teaching negotiation, instead of just watching their posts.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel on being asked for an a-year-ago list?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel curious and encouraged to try it too, measuring progress against Chinmay's own past instead of the reunion group.

grounding: A young professional measures progress against a year ago, mutes accounts that bring them down and learns from a few chosen peers.

passage: All through the Delhi winter, Sonali's tuition teacher said the same thing: "Slow as a tortoise, this one." He said it whenever she took long over sums. Next to her sat Tenzin, whom he called "our little genius". By January the difference showed. When the teacher wrote a hard puzzle on the board "for extra marks", Tenzin's hand shot up; he tried it three different ways, got it wrong twice and kept going. Sonali didn't even copy it down. What was the point? Tortoises didn't get extra marks. In the auto on the way home through the fog, her mother asked how tuition went. "I'm slow," Sonali said, as if it were her name. Her mother turned round. "Who says?" Sonali shrugged and looked out at the fog.

qa.q: What did the tuition teacher call Tenzin?
qa.a: "Our little genius."

qa.q: Why didn't Sonali even copy down the hard puzzle?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and hopeless, having come to believe the "slow" label, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could Sonali's mother do next?
qa.a: She could talk gently with Sonali about what she is good at, ask the teacher to stop using the label, and praise her effort on hard problems.

qa.q: How does being called "our little genius" affect Tenzin?
qa.a: It gives Tenzin the confidence to attempt hard puzzles and keep going after getting them wrong twice.

grounding: A child repeatedly called slow stops trying while a classmate called clever takes on hard puzzles, each living up to the label.
